summary.text: Two integrations by parts give a recurrence for the normalized integrals \(J_m/m!\), and matching its initial values identifies these integrals (up to sign) with the odd-index errors. Since \(|x^2-x|\leq 1/4\) on \([0,1]\), the integral errors decay geometrically; the original recurrence transfers the bound to even indices, and the denominators are at least \(1\), so the ratio errors tend to zero.

full_proof.text:
Let \(e=\exp(1)\). Write \(a_n\) for A340737 and \(b_n\) for A340738. Thus
\[
a_1=3,\quad a_2=5,\qquad b_1=1,\quad b_2=2,
\]
and both sequences obey the same recurrence: for \(n\ge 3\),
\[
x_n=\begin{cases}
2x_{n-1}+nx_{n-2},&n\text{ odd},\\[2mm]
\dfrac{n+2}{2}x_{n-1}-x_{n-2}-\dfrac{n-2}{2}x_{n-3},&n\text{ even}.
\end{cases}
\]
(The definitions also assign the irrelevant value \(0\) at index \(0\).) We prove that \(a_n/b_n\to e\).

It is useful first to treat both sequences by one integer-valued recurrence. Given integers \(p,q\), define \(G_n=G_n(p,q)\) by
\[
G_0=0,\qquad G_1=p,\qquad G_2=q,
\]
and by the displayed recurrence above for \(n\ge3\). In terms of parity, the two parts of this recurrence become, for every \(j\ge0\),
\[
G_{2j+3}=2G_{2j+2}+(2j+3)G_{2j+1},                                      \tag{1}
\]
\[
G_{2j+4}=(j+3)G_{2j+3}-G_{2j+2}-(j+1)G_{2j+1}.                            \tag{2}
\]

We need two elementary facts about this recurrence. If \(0\le p\le q\), then
\[
0\le G_n\le G_{n+1}\qquad(n\ge0).                                       \tag{3}
\]
This follows by strong induction. It is immediate for the initial pairs \((G_0,G_1)=(0,p)\) and \((G_1,G_2)=(p,q)\). Also
\[
G_3=2q+3p\ge q=G_2.
\]
For the general induction step, suppose all needed preceding terms are nonnegative and increasing. Equation (1) makes \(G_{2j+3}\) nonnegative. Moreover, using (2),
\[
\begin{aligned}
G_{2j+4}-G_{2j+3}
 &= (j+2)G_{2j+3}-G_{2j+2}-(j+1)G_{2j+1}\\
 &= (G_{2j+3}-G_{2j+2})
    +(j+1)(G_{2j+3}-G_{2j+1})\ge0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Conversely, when establishing the next pair beginning with an even index, (2) can be rearranged as
\[
G_{2j+4}=(j+1)(G_{2j+3}-G_{2j+1})+(2G_{2j+3}-G_{2j+2}),
\]
which is nonnegative because the preceding terms are nonnegative and increasing. Finally, applying (1) with \(j+1\),
\[
G_{2j+5}=2G_{2j+4}+(2j+5)G_{2j+3},
\]
so both \(G_{2j+5}\ge0\) and \(G_{2j+5}-G_{2j+4}\ge0\). This completes the induction and proves (3).

Consequently, for the initial data used here, all the expressions in the even recurrence are nonnegative. Thus the natural-number subtraction in the definitions of the OEIS sequences agrees with ordinary integer subtraction, and induction on the index gives
\[
a_n=G_n(3,5),\qquad b_n=G_n(1,2).                                       \tag{4}
\]
In particular, (3) applied to \((p,q)=(1,2)\) gives
\[
b_n\ge b_1=1\qquad(n\ge1).                                             \tag{5}
\]

We next extract a recurrence involving only odd-indexed terms. Substitute (2) into (1) with \(j=k+1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
G_{2k+5}
 &=2G_{2k+4}+(2k+5)G_{2k+3}\\
 &=2\bigl((k+3)G_{2k+3}-G_{2k+2}-(k+1)G_{2k+1}\bigr)
   +(2k+5)G_{2k+3}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Equation (1) at \(j=k\) says \(2G_{2k+2}=G_{2k+3}-(2k+3)G_{2k+1}\). Using this in the preceding expression and collecting terms yields
\[
G_{2k+5}=(4k+10)G_{2k+3}+G_{2k+1}.                                      \tag{6}
\]

We now construct a small quantity satisfying exactly this recurrence. For \(m\ge0\), define
\[
J_m=\int_0^1 (t^2-t)^m e^t\,dt
\]
and also
\[
W_m=\int_0^1 (t^2-t)^m(2t-1)e^t\,dt.
\]
We derive two integration-by-parts identities. Put \(u=t^2-t\), so \(u'=2t-1\). The derivative of \(u^{m+1}e^t\) is
\[
(m+1)u^m(2t-1)e^t+u^{m+1}e^t.
\]
Since \(u=0\) at both \(t=0\) and \(t=1\), integrating this derivative over \([0,1]\) gives
\[
J_{m+1}=-(m+1)W_m.                                                       \tag{7}
\]

For the second identity, differentiate \(u^{m+1}(2t-1)e^t\). This gives
\[
(m+1)u^m(2t-1)^2e^t+2u^{m+1}e^t+u^{m+1}(2t-1)e^t.
\]
The elementary identity
\[
(2t-1)^2=4(t^2-t)+1=4u+1
\]
turns this derivative into
\[
(4m+6)u^{m+1}e^t+(m+1)u^me^t+u^{m+1}(2t-1)e^t.
\]
Again the differentiated function vanishes at both endpoints. Integration therefore gives
\[
W_{m+1}=-(4m+6)J_{m+1}-(m+1)J_m.                                       \tag{8}
\]
Applying (7) with \(m+1\), and then substituting (8), yields the three-term recurrence
\[
J_{m+2}=(4m+6)(m+2)J_{m+1}+(m+1)(m+2)J_m.                               \tag{9}
\]

Normalize by factorials:
\[
F_m=\frac{J_m}{m!}.
\]
Dividing (9) by \((m+2)!=(m+2)(m+1)m!\) gives
\[
F_{m+2}=(4m+6)F_{m+1}+F_m.                                              \tag{10}
\]

The first integral values are also explicit. Direct integration gives
\[
J_0=\int_0^1e^t\,dt=e-1.                                                \tag{11}
\]
For \(J_1\), observe that
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\bigl((t^2-3t+3)e^t\bigr)=(t^2-t)e^t.
\]
Evaluating at the endpoints gives
\[
J_1=e-3.                                                               \tag{12}
\]
Using (9) with \(m=0\),
\[
J_2=12J_1+2J_0=14e-38.                                                  \tag{13}
\]

We also need a uniform estimate for these integrals. On \([0,1]\),
\[
|t^2-t|=t(1-t)\le\frac14,
\]
where the last inequality follows, for example, from \((t-\tfrac12)^2\ge0\). Also \(e^t\le e\). Hence
\[
|J_m|
 \le \int_0^1 |t^2-t|^m e^t\,dt
 \le \int_0^1 e\left(\frac14\right)^m dt
 =e\left(\frac14\right)^m.                                             \tag{14}
\]

Consider now the error at odd indices:
\[
\rho_k=G_{2k+1}(3,5)-eG_{2k+1}(1,2).
\]
By applying (6) to both terms, we find
\[
\rho_{k+2}=(4k+10)\rho_{k+1}+\rho_k.                                   \tag{15}
\]
The first two values are
\[
\rho_0=3-e.
\]
Furthermore, (1) gives \(G_3(3,5)=2\cdot5+3\cdot3=19\) and
\(G_3(1,2)=2\cdot2+3\cdot1=7\), so
\[
\rho_1=19-7e.                                                          \tag{16}
\]

We claim the exact identity
\[
\rho_k=-F_{k+1}=-\frac{J_{k+1}}{(k+1)!}.                                \tag{17}
\]
For \(k=0\), this follows from (12): \(-F_1=-(e-3)=3-e\). For \(k=1\), (13) gives
\[
-F_2=-\frac{14e-38}{2}=19-7e.
\]
Finally, if (17) holds for \(k\) and \(k+1\), then (10), used with index \(m=k+1\), says
\[
F_{k+3}=(4k+10)F_{k+2}+F_{k+1}.
\]
After negating, this is precisely recurrence (15). Thus induction proves (17) for every \(k\).

Because \((k+1)!\ge1\), (14) and (17) imply the particularly convenient bound
\[
|\rho_k|\le e\left(\frac14\right)^{k+1}.                               \tag{18}
\]
We now convert this odd-index estimate into one valid at every index.

First let \(n=2k+1\) be odd. By definition, the error \(G_n(3,5)-eG_n(1,2)\) is \(\rho_k\), so (18) gives
\[
|G_n(3,5)-eG_n(1,2)|\le e4^{-(k+1)}.
\]
Since
\[
e4^{-(k+1)}\le (2k+2)e\,2^{-(2k+1)},
\]
we obtain
\[
|G_n(3,5)-eG_n(1,2)|
 \le (n+1)e\left(\frac12\right)^n.                                     \tag{19}
\]
(The displayed comparison reduces to \(1/4\le k+1\).)

Next let \(n=2j+2\) be positive and even. Apply (1) separately to \(G(3,5)\) and \(G(1,2)\), then subtract \(e\) times the second equality from the first. In terms of the errors this says
\[
\rho_{j+1}=2\bigl(G_{2j+2}(3,5)-eG_{2j+2}(1,2)\bigr)+(2j+3)\rho_j.
\]
Therefore
\[
G_{2j+2}(3,5)-eG_{2j+2}(1,2)
 =\frac{\rho_{j+1}-(2j+3)\rho_j}{2}.                                    \tag{20}
\]
Using the triangle inequality and (18),
\[
\begin{aligned}
|G_{2j+2}(3,5)-eG_{2j+2}(1,2)|
&\le \frac12\left(|\rho_{j+1}|+(2j+3)|\rho_j|\right)\\
&\le \frac e2\left(4^{-(j+2)}+(2j+3)4^{-(j+1)}\right)\\
&=e4^{-(j+1)}\left(\frac18+\frac{2j+3}{2}\right)\\
&\le (2j+3)e4^{-(j+1)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last inequality is equivalent to \(\frac18+\frac{2j+3}{2}\le2j+3\), which is immediate for \(j\ge0\). Since \(4^{-(j+1)}=2^{-(2j+2)}\), this is again exactly
\[
|G_n(3,5)-eG_n(1,2)|
 \le(n+1)e\left(\frac12\right)^n.                                      \tag{21}
\]
Combining (19) and (21), for every \(n\ge1\),
\[
|G_n(3,5)-eG_n(1,2)|
 \le(n+1)e\left(\frac12\right)^n.                                      \tag{22}
\]

Using (4), (5), and \(b_n>0\), we can divide by the denominator:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left|\frac{a_n}{b_n}-e\right|
 &=\frac{|a_n-eb_n|}{b_n}\\
 &\le |a_n-eb_n|\\
 &\le(n+1)e\left(\frac12\right)^n.                                     \tag{23}
\end{aligned}
\]
Finally,
\[
(n+1)e\left(\frac12\right)^n
=e\left(n\left(\frac12\right)^n+\left(\frac12\right)^n\right)
\longrightarrow0.
\]
Indeed, the geometric term \(2^{-n}\) tends to zero, and so does \(n2^{-n}\) (for example, this is the standard fact that a polynomial factor is dominated by geometric decay). Equation (23) and the squeeze theorem therefore imply
\[
\frac{a_n}{b_n}\longrightarrow e.
\]
Thus the A340737 numerators divided by the corresponding A340738 denominators converge to Euler's number.
